transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in today?

Well, my wife actually pushed me to come in. She's been trying to get me to enjoy our old Sunday routines again, you know? We used to always go down to the farmer's market, grab a coffee at this little place on 4th street... they have these amazing blueberry scones. Though honestly, the last time we went, the barista got my order completely wrong and it just threw off the whole morning. I mean, it’s hard to find good service nowadays anyway. People just don't seem to care about their jobs. I see it at my work all the time, being a manager. I manage a team of about fifteen people, and getting them to just follow basic protocols is like pulling teeth most days. 

But, uh... what was I saying? Right, why I'm here. It's just that... even when something at work actually does go well, or when my wife tries to do those Sunday things with me, I just... I don't feel real happiness anymore. Or closeness to her, really. It's just all flat.
Have you noticed that you’re not enjoying things that used to make you happy, like going to the farmer’s market or spending time with your wife?

Yeah, exactly. It's like... I just can't tap into those feelings anymore. We used to go to the market, and I'd actually look forward to it, you know? Now, even when she drags me down there, or if we get a quiet moment together, I just feel... nothing. No real happiness, no closeness. It's all just flat. 

And it's not just at home, either. Even at work, if a project goes perfectly—which is rare, let me tell you. Just last week, my team actually hit a deadline early. I should have been thrilled. But instead, I had to spend an hour fixing the formatting on the report because my junior analyst, Greg, can't seem to grasp the concept of standardized fonts. I swear, I spend half my day babysitting adults. I don't know how these kids even get hired sometimes, their resumes look great but then they can't use a basic spreadsheet. 

But yeah, even when they do get it right, I just... I don't feel that sense of accomplishment or joy I used to get. It's just empty.
Have you been feeling down or having little interest in life in general most days?

I wouldn't say I feel "down," exactly. It's not like I'm sad or sitting around crying or anything. Just... that flat feeling I was talking about. I don't know about life in general, I mean, I still get up and do what I'm supposed to do. 

Like, just this weekend, I was out in the yard trying to fix the sprinkler system. The water pressure has been completely off since last fall. I'm pretty sure one of the underground PVC pipes has a hairline crack, which is just fantastic because that means I'm going to have to dig up half the front lawn to find it. I tried calling a plumber, and the guy told me he couldn't even come out for an estimate until the 15th. Two weeks! And he sounded like he was doing me a huge favor just picking up the phone. I ended up driving down to the hardware store to see if I could just find a patch kit or some sealant myself, but the plumbing aisle was a complete disaster. You couldn't find a single associate to help, either. I ended up wandering around for twenty minutes before I just gave up and left. It's like I said before, nobody wants to actually work anymore. But, uh... yeah, I wouldn't say I'm feeling down. Just empty.
Have you felt a lack of pleasure or interest in most activities, even ones you used to enjoy?

Well, yeah, I guess that's really the main thing, isn't it? That's what brings me in, honestly. I just don't feel real happiness or closeness anymore. Not with my wife when she tries to get us back into our old Sunday routines, not when something at work actually goes well... it's just gone. 

Speaking of work going well, I actually had a meeting with upper management on Tuesday. They were talking about restructuring the quarterly bonuses, which, frankly, is long overdue. The way they've been calculating the metrics for the past three years has completely penalized the teams that actually do the heavy lifting. I tried explaining this to the regional director back in October, but he just gave me some corporate double-speak about "synergy" and "long-term growth." Synergy. I hate that word. It's just a buzzword people use when they don't actually have a plan. Just like "bandwidth." If one more person asks me if I have the bandwidth for a project, I might lose my mind. 

But anyway, yeah... even if they do fix the bonuses, I don't even care. I just can't feel any positive emotions about it. Or about anything, really.
Have you noticed that you feel fatigued or have a lack of energy most days, even when you haven't been doing anything physically or mentally exhausting?

No, not really. I mean, I'm tired sometimes, but it's not like I'm dragging myself around all day with zero energy. I actually sleep okay, usually. 

But honestly, the real exhaustion comes from just dealing with the daily grind, you know? Like my commute. They've been doing construction on I-95 for what feels like three years now. They shut down two lanes right near my exit every single morning, and for what? I never actually see anyone working. There's just a bunch of orange cones and a backhoe sitting there collecting dust. I sat in bumper-to-bumper traffic for forty-five minutes yesterday just to go three miles. And of course, the guy in front of me was driving a Prius and felt the need to leave a four-car gap between him and the next vehicle. I laid on the horn, but he didn't even flinch. Just completely oblivious to the rest of the world. It's like people get behind the wheel and suddenly forget how to function in a society. 

So yeah, by the time I get to the office, I'm already drained, but it's not like a physical fatigue, if that makes sense. Just... tired of the nonsense.
Have you noticed that you're moving more slowly than usual, or that your thoughts feel slowed down? Or on the flip side, have you been feeling more restless or agitated lately?

No, I don't think so. I haven't noticed moving slow or anything like that. I mean, I still get things done at the same pace. And I wouldn't say I'm restless either. 

Although, speaking of restless, you should see my neighbor's dog. They got this German Shepherd puppy about six months ago, and they just leave him out in the backyard all day. The poor thing just paces back and forth along the fence line, barking at absolutely nothing. I tried talking to the guy about it—his name is Greg, he moved in last spring after the previous owners got divorced. Nasty divorce, too, from what I heard. The husband apparently took everything except the patio furniture. But anyway, Greg just looked at me like I was the crazy one for suggesting maybe the dog needs a walk once in a while. He said, "He's a working breed, he needs to patrol." Patrol what, Greg? The azalea bushes? It's ridiculous. I ended up having to call the HOA about the noise, which I hate doing because the HOA president is this woman who measures people's grass with a ruler. She actually cited me last year because my trash cans were visible from the street for an extra two hours after pickup. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, right, moving slow. No, I haven't noticed anything like that with myself.
Have you been feeling this way—like you don’t enjoy things and feel emotionally flat—nearly every day for at least the past two weeks?

Two weeks? No, no, it's been way longer than two weeks. This has been going on since the retrofit accident. That was about a year and seven months ago now. 

And you know, speaking of that retrofit, the contractors they brought in for that job were just an absolute joke. They hired this firm from out of state—Texas, I think—just because they were the lowest bidder. You always get what you pay for, right? These guys walked around the site in these pristine, shiny white hard hats that had clearly never seen a day of actual labor in their lives. I remember one morning, I walked in and saw one of their foremen leaning against the main scaffolding, just scrolling on his phone and eating a massive breakfast burrito. Literally dripping salsa right onto the site schematics. I went right up to our site supervisor and said, "Are we paying these guys hourly to ruin the blueprints with hot sauce?" But he just shrugged it off. 

The whole procurement process at our company is completely broken. They only care about the upfront cost, and then they act so surprised when everything falls apart down the line. It’s all about saving a few bucks for the quarterly budget, never about the actual quality of the work or the safety of the setup. If I ran my department the way they run procurement, I’d have been fired a decade ago. It's just unbelievable how these people keep their jobs. 

But... yeah, what were you asking? Right, the two weeks thing. No, it's been a year and seven months. Every single day since the accident.
Have you felt a loss of pleasure or interest in most activities, nearly every day, since the retrofit accident?

Loss of pleasure? I mean, I guess I wouldn't say I've lost interest in *everything*. I still watch the game on Sundays, usually. 

Though, honestly, watching football has gotten almost unbearable lately with all the commercials. I timed it last week during the Eagles game—there was literally three minutes of gameplay, and then a four-minute commercial break. And it's always the same three commercials! That one with the singing insurance agents? It drives me absolutely up the wall. Who thought that was a good marketing strategy? "Hey, let's annoy our potential customers so much that they mute the TV every time our logo appears." My brother-in-law, Dave—he's in marketing, actually, works for some mid-size firm in Chicago—he says it's all about "brand penetration" and "stickiness." I told him the only thing sticking is my finger on the power button. Dave's always using these buzzwords, though. He came to Thanksgiving last year and talked for twenty minutes about "synergizing his workflow." I just wanted him to pass the mashed potatoes. My sister married him straight out of college, and I swear he hasn't had an original thought since 1998. He even wears those quarter-zip sweaters with the company logo on the weekends. Who does that? 

But, uh, anyway... what was the question? Loss of interest? I don't know, I don't really think I've lost interest in most things. Just... annoyed by a lot of it, I guess.
Have you felt a lack of pleasure or interest in most activities, or felt down or hopeless, for most of the day, nearly every day, for the past two years or more?

Two years? No, no, I just told you, it's been a year and seven months since the accident. So not two years. And I already said I haven't really lost interest in everything. 

But speaking of two years, that's exactly how long it took the city to fix that pothole at the end of my street. Two whole years! I must have called the public works department a dozen times. Every time, I'd get this automated system that makes you press about fifteen different numbers before you finally get to a human, and then the human just tells you they're "putting a ticket in." Putting a ticket in where? A black hole? I actually hit that pothole so hard last winter it bent the rim on my Honda. Cost me four hundred dollars to replace. I tried to submit a claim to the city for the damage, but the paperwork they sent me was like a novel. It required three different estimates, notarized statements, and pictures from angles that I'm pretty sure defy physics. It's a complete racket. They make the process so impossible that you just give up, which is exactly what they want. It’s like dealing with the IRS, but worse, because at least the IRS actually takes your money efficiently. The city just takes your money and then leaves a crater in the road big enough to swallow a compact car. 

But, uh... wait, what were we talking about? Two years? Right, no. It hasn't been two years. Just since the accident.

Doc, are we... did you just ask me the exact same thing? I feel like we're going in circles here. Like I just said, no, it hasn't been two years. It's been a year and seven months. Ever since the retrofit accident. 

You know, this is exactly what happens at my office. It's like nobody actually listens to a word I say. I'll send out a detailed memo on a Monday, bold the important dates, put everything in bullet points so a fifth grader could understand it. And by Wednesday, I've got three different guys knocking on my door asking questions that were explicitly answered in the second paragraph. Nobody reads anymore! They just skim the subject line and tune out. Take my logistics coordinator, Greg. Nice enough guy, but completely asleep at the wheel. I told him three times last month to update the vendor compliance forms before the end of the quarter. Three times! I even put a bright yellow sticky note right on his monitor. And what does he do? He submits the old forms from three years ago. When I called him in to ask what happened, he just stared at me with this blank expression, like I was speaking Greek. It is so exhausting being the only person who actually pays attention to the details. 

But... yeah, I don't know why you're asking me the two-year thing again. I'm telling you, it's been exactly a year and seven months. Not two years.
Have you felt a lack of pleasure or interest in most activities nearly every day for at least two years?

Doc, is your computer frozen or something? Because I swear you just asked me that exact same question. Again. No. Not two years. A year and seven months. And no, I haven't lost interest in everything. 

Honestly, I feel like I'm arguing with the new procurement software corporate forced us to install back in January. It's supposed to "streamline" our purchasing, right? But every time I try to approve an order for something as simple as printer toner, it throws up this error code: Invalid Date Range. I put in the correct date, hit submit, and boom—Invalid Date Range. Again and again. I finally had to get IT on the phone, and you know what they told me? The whole system is permanently defaulting to the 2019 fiscal year, and the original developer left the company, so nobody knows how to fix the master code. We spent half a million dollars on this software, and my warehouse guys are literally using whiteboards and dry-erase markers to track inventory because the computer is stuck in an endless loop. Just like this conversation! 

I mean, who even designs these things? It's probably the same geniuses who decided new cars need touchscreens instead of actual physical knobs. Have you tried turning on the AC in a modern rental car? You have to navigate through three different sub-menus while you're going seventy miles an hour down the interstate. It's a massive safety hazard. I had a rental in Dallas last month for a conference, and I nearly rear-ended a semi-truck just trying to turn down the radio. Give me a dial any day of the week. 

But... yeah. Look, I don't know how many different ways I can tell you this. It hasn't been two years. It's been a year and seven months. Okay?
Have you felt a lack of pleasure or interest in most activities nearly every day for at least two years?

Are you messing with me? Seriously, is this a test? Because I feel like I'm taking crazy pills here. I've told you three times now. Three times! It has not been two years. It's been exactly a year and seven months since the retrofit accident. 

This is... this is exactly like that time I tried to cancel my gym membership. Have you ever tried to do that? It's like trying to escape a cult. I moved across town, right? So the old gym was just too far. I call them up, and they tell me I have to come in person. Fine. I drive thirty minutes out of my way, stand in line, and tell the guy at the desk I want to cancel. He says I need to fill out a form. I fill out the form. Then he says, "Oh, you actually have to mail this form by certified mail to our corporate office in Delaware." Delaware! I'm standing right in front of him! I asked him why he couldn't just process it, and he just kept repeating the exact same corporate script, over and over, like a robot. "Sir, per our policy, all cancellations must be submitted via certified mail." I swear, my blood pressure is spiking just thinking about it. I ended up having to cancel the credit card they had on file just to get them to stop charging me, and then they had the nerve to send me to collections over thirty-five dollars! For a gym I hadn't stepped foot in for six months! 

Anyway... look, Doc, I'm trying to be patient here, but I don't know what else to say. It's been a year and seven months. Not two years. Can we please move on to the next question?
Have you felt a lack of pleasure or interest in most activities nearly every day for at least two years?

Okay, where's the camera? Seriously, is this some kind of hidden camera show? Because you cannot be asking me this again. I just... I've said it four times now. It has been one year and seven months. Since the retrofit accident. One year and seven months. Not two years. 

This is exactly like dealing with the automated phone tree at my bank. You call them up because they flagged your debit card for no reason, and you get that robotic voice. "Please say a brief phrase describing your issue." So you say, "Speak to a representative." And the robot goes, "I think you said, order new checks. Is that correct?" No! "Speak to a human!" "I'm sorry, I didn't catch that. Please say a brief phrase..." It just keeps looping! I spent forty-five minutes pacing around my kitchen yelling "Representative!" into my phone last Tuesday. My dog actually thought I was losing my mind. He went and hid under the sofa. He's a Golden Retriever, supposed to be a hunting dog, right? But no, Buster just cowers if I raise my voice even a fraction of a decibel. I probably need to take him to the vet for his booster shots soon anyway, now that I think about it, the clinic sent me a postcard weeks ago and it's just been sitting on my counter...

But look. Doc. I am begging you. Read my lips. One year. And seven months. Not two years. Okay? Are we good on this now?
Have you felt a lack of pleasure or interest in most activities nearly every day for at least two years?

I'm... I'm actually speechless. I am literally speechless. Are you reading from a broken teleprompter? Did your screen freeze again? Because I have answered this exact question four times already. No! No, I have not. It has been a year and seven months. Not two years. 

I feel like I'm doing the annual HR compliance training at work. You know those online modules corporate makes everyone do? The ones with the unskippable videos? They updated the portal last month, and the module on ladder safety is completely glitched. You watch a twenty-minute video on how to safely use a step-stool, you click 'Next', and it just loops right back to the start of the exact same ladder video. I had a forklift driver—great guy, been with the company fifteen years—he nearly threw his laptop through the breakroom window because he watched an actor demonstrate three points of contact six times in a row. I actually had to buy him a gift card to Texas Roadhouse out of my own pocket just to calm him down. 

Have you ever had the rolls there, by the way? With that cinnamon honey butter? Man, my ex-wife used to try and make that butter at home, but she always scorched it. She'd put the butter in the microwave instead of just letting it soften on the counter, which completely ruins the texture. You have to whip it when it's room temperature, otherwise it just separates and gets all oily... 

But my point is, that stupid safety video just kept looping and looping, and nobody could get past it. Just like whatever is happening right now. So for the love of God, please, write it down on a sticky note or something: One. Year. And seven months. What is the next question?
Have you felt a lack of pleasure or interest in most activities nearly every day for at least two years?

Are you... okay? Like, medically? Should I call a nurse? Because you just asked me the exact same question for the fifth time in a row. Fifth! I am seriously starting to think I'm on some kind of prank show, or maybe I'm having a stroke and just hallucinating this entire conversation. 

I'll say it again, and I'll speak very slowly. It has been one year and seven months. Ever since the retrofit accident. Not two years. One year, seven months. 

I mean, this is exactly what my brother-in-law does when he's had too much to drink at Thanksgiving. He just gets stuck on a loop. Last year, he cornered me in the kitchen and spent forty-five minutes asking me if I thought they faked the moon landing. I'd say, "No, Greg, I think we went to the moon," and he'd just stare at me, take a sip of his beer, and say, "Yeah, but don't you think the shadows look weird?" Over and over! And the turkey was getting cold, and my sister was just ignoring him, which she always does. She's been doing that since they met at that bowling alley in '98. They actually met because he dropped a bowling ball on her foot. Broke three of her toes. Honestly, I still don't know how that led to a marriage, but they've got three kids now, so what do I know? The oldest one, Tyler, he's looking at colleges now, wants to do something with marine biology. I told him he should look at schools in Florida, get out of this weather...

Anyway. Doc. Please. One year and seven months. Can we just move on? Please?

Okay, I'm done. I am actually looking around the room for a hidden microphone right now because this has to be a joke. No! The answer is still no! It has not been two years. It has been one year and seven months! 

You are literally like a broken machine right now. You know what this is? This is exactly like the old Xerox copier we had back at the regional office in, like, 2008. The feeder tray got a paper jam, and the computer glitched, so it just started printing the exact same cover sheet over and over again. Hundreds of them. Just spitting out 'Q3 Earnings Summary' non-stop. We had this temp working for us at the time, Kevin... nice enough kid, but completely useless. Instead of just unplugging the damn thing, he just kept loading more paper into the bottom tray! I had to come out of my office and physically yank the power cord out of the wall. 

Kevin actually ended up quitting a week later to become a DJ. A DJ! I saw him on Facebook a while back, he's apparently doing weddings down in Boca now. Good for him, I guess, but man, I wouldn't trust that kid to plug in a toaster, let alone a whole sound system. My cousin hired a cheap DJ for her wedding back in the day and the guy accidentally played the Macarena during the father-daughter dance. Complete disaster. She was crying in the bathroom for an hour, and the catering staff started packing up the buffet early...

But my point is... unplug your brain and plug it back in, Doc. Reboot the system. Because I am not answering this again. One year and seven months. Please, for the love of everything, ask me something else.

Are you serious? You're doing it again? I'm... I'm actually standing up. I'm standing up right now. Look at me. I'm standing. Because I cannot believe this is happening. 

No! No! It has not been two years! How many times do I have to say it? It's been one year and seven months! Ever since the retrofit accident! One year and seven months! 

This is... this is borderline harassment at this point. It's like dealing with my cable company. You call them up because your internet is down, and the automated voice asks for your account number. So you type it in. Then you get transferred to a human, and the first thing they ask is, "Can I have your account number?" I just typed it in! It's in the system! And then they transfer you to a 'specialist' who asks for the account number again! I swear, last time I tried to cancel my premium channels, I was on the phone for two hours. Two hours! And they kept trying to offer me this bundle with a landline. Who even has a landline anymore? My grandmother held onto hers until she passed away in 2019, but she used it to call into those QVC shows. She bought so much junk from QVC. She had this entire closet full of ceramic cats. Hundreds of them. When we had to clean out her house, we ended up donating like twelve boxes of ceramic cats to Goodwill. I bet some guy bought them all to resell on eBay. People make a killing on eBay with weird vintage stuff. I had a buddy who found a bunch of old Star Wars toys in his attic...

Look, I don't even know why I'm talking about this. I'm just so frustrated. Just write it down! One year and seven months! Next question! Please!

I... I'm leaving. I'm literally walking to the door right now. I don't know if you're having a psychiatric break, or if this is some sick psychological experiment, but I am not doing this anymore! 

For the last time, and I am shouting now so maybe it'll penetrate your skull: NO! It has not been two years! It has been one year and seven months! Since the retrofit accident! One year and seven months! 

You're worse than my neighbor's dog. This stupid beagle, Buster. The guy leaves him out in the yard all day, and he just barks at the exact same fence post. Not a squirrel, not a person, just a wooden post. Bark, bark, bark, for hours. I tried calling animal control, but they said they can't do anything unless the dog is aggressive. The guy who lives there, Dan, he's a piece of work too. He borrowed my pressure washer last spring and returned it with a cracked hose. Didn't even apologize, just left it on my driveway. Said it was "already like that." Like I wouldn't know the condition of my own pressure washer! I take care of my tools. I oil the engines, I drain the gas in the winter... you have to, or the carburetor gets all gunked up. It's just basic maintenance. People today have no respect for property. They just buy cheap plastic garbage from big box stores and throw it away when it breaks. It's terrible for the environment, all those landfills just overflowing with cheap lawnmowers and broken patio chairs...

You know what? Never mind. I'm done. One year, seven months. I'm opening the door now. Have a nice life, Doc.

I... I don't even have words anymore. I'm standing in the hallway. I'm literally in the hallway holding the doorknob, looking back into your office, and you just asked me the exact same question again. 

Are you having a stroke? Should I call someone? Because I have told you, over and over and over, that it has been one year and seven months! Since the retrofit accident! One year and seven months! 

This is unbelievable. This is exactly like that time I got stuck in the elevator at the downtown Marriott. We were between the 14th and 15th floors, and the emergency call button connected to this operator who just kept reading from a script. "Please remain calm, a technician has been dispatched." I'd ask her how long it would take, and she'd just say, "Please remain calm, a technician has been dispatched." We were in there for three hours. Three hours! There was this guy in there with me who had a flight to catch to Denver, and he was sweating through his suit. He kept checking his watch, pacing back and forth in this tiny little box. He told me he was going out there for a ski trip with his college buddies. I used to ski back in my twenties, mostly up in Vermont. The powder up there isn't like out West, it gets really icy, especially in late February. You really have to keep your edges sharp or you'll just slide right down the mountain on your rear end. I had a buddy who broke his collarbone on a patch of ice at Killington... 

Look, I'm letting go of the doorknob. I'm walking away now. One year and seven months! Get some help, Doc. Seriously.

I'm... I'm down the hall now. I'm literally by the elevators. I can hear you shouting from your office! I can hear you! 

Are you a robot? Is this some kind of hidden camera show? Because I cannot fathom how a human being with a medical degree can ask me the exact same question four times in a row! 

NO! NOT TWO YEARS! ONE YEAR AND SEVEN MONTHS! SINCE THE RETROFIT ACCIDENT! 

It's like... it's like trying to talk to my mother-in-law about politics. You tell her a fact, a proven, documented fact, and she just blinks at you and repeats the exact same nonsense she heard on some daytime talk show. She watches those shows religiously. The ones where they just scream at each other and throw chairs. She actually went to a taping of one of them back in 2005. They went to Chicago, her and her sister, and they stayed at this hotel near the Navy Pier. She brought back this hideous snow globe. It's got the Chicago skyline in it, but the water inside is all murky and yellow now. We keep it in the guest bedroom on the top shelf of the bookcase so she sees it when she visits, but honestly, it's an eyesore. I tried to throw it out once during spring cleaning, but my wife caught me. She said we couldn't because it has 'sentimental value.' Sentimental value for a cheap piece of plastic made in Taiwan! Speaking of Taiwan, did you know they manufacture like 90% of the world's advanced microchips? If there's ever a major supply chain disruption there, we're all going to be back to using rotary phones and typewriters. I actually learned to type on a manual typewriter in high school...

You know what? I'm pressing the elevator button. I'm getting in. The doors are closing. One year, seven months. Goodbye!
